Main.sentence: Chlorine is a ___E:chemical element U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_element)___ ; it has ___E:symbol U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symbol_(chemistry))___ Cl and ___E:atomic number U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_number)___ 17. The second-lightest of the ___E:halogens U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halogen)___ , it appears between ___E:fluorine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fluorine)___ and ___E:bromine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bromine)___ in the periodic table and its properties are mostly intermediate between them. Chlorine is a yellow-green gas at room temperature.

It is an extremely reactive element and a strong ___E:oxidising agent U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxidizing_agent)___ : among the elements, it has the highest ___E:electron affinity U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electron_affinity)___ and the third-highest ___E:electronegativity U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronegativity)___ on the revised ___E:Pauling scale U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronegativity#Pauling_electronegativity)___ , behind only ___E:oxygen U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygen)___ and fluorine.

Chlorine played an important role in the experiments conducted by medieval ___E:alchemists U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alchemy)___ , which commonly involved the heating of chloride ___E:salts U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salt_(chemistry))___ like ___E:ammonium chloride U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ammonium_chloride)___ ( ___E:sal ammoniac U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sal_ammoniac)___ ) and ___E:sodium chloride U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodium_chloride)___ ( ___E:common salt U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_salt)___ ), producing various chemical substances containing chlorine such as ___E:hydrogen chloride U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen_chloride)___ , ___E:mercury(II) chloride U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury(II)_chloride)___ (corrosive sublimate), and aqua regia .

However, the nature of free chlorine gas as a separate substance was only recognised around 1630 by ___E:Jan Baptist van Helmont U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Baptist_van_Helmont)___ . ___E:Carl Wilhelm Scheele U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Wilhelm_Scheele)___ wrote a description of chlorine gas in 1774, supposing it to be an ___E:oxide U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxide)___ of a new element.

In 1809, chemists suggested that the gas might be a pure element, and this was confirmed by ___E:Sir Humphry Davy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_Humphry_Davy)___ in 1810, who named it after the ___E:Ancient Greek U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Greek_language)___ χλωρός ( khlōrós , "pale green") because of its colour.

Because of its great reactivity, all chlorine in the Earth's crust is in the form of ___E:ionic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ion)___ ___E:chloride U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chloride)___ compounds, which includes table salt. It is the ___E:second-most abundant U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abundance_of_elements_in_Earth%27s_crust)___ halogen (after fluorine) and 20th most abundant element in Earth's crust.
These crystal deposits are nevertheless dwarfed by the huge reserves of chloride in seawater.

Elemental chlorine is commercially produced from ___E:brine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brine)___ by ___E:electrolysis U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrolysis)___ , predominantly in the ___E:chloralkali process U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chloralkali_process)___ .

The high oxidising potential of elemental chlorine led to the development of commercial ___E:bleaches U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bleach_(chemical))___ and ___E:disinfectants U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disinfectant)___ , and a ___E:reagent U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reagent)___ for many processes in the chemical industry.

Chlorine is used in the manufacture of a wide range of consumer products, about two-thirds of them organic chemicals such as ___E:polyvinyl chloride U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polyvinyl_chloride)___ (PVC), many intermediates for the production of ___E:plastics U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plastics)___ , and other end products which do not contain the element.

As a common disinfectant, elemental chlorine and chlorine-generating compounds are used more directly in ___E:swimming pools U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swimming_pool)___ to keep them ___E:sanitary U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swimming_pool_sanitation)___ .

Elemental chlorine at high ___E:concentration U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concentration)___ is extremely dangerous, and ___E:poisonous U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poisonous)___ to most living organisms.

As a ___E:chemical warfare U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_warfare)___ agent, chlorine was first used in ___E:World War I U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I)___ as a ___E:poison gas U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poison_gas)___ weapon.

In the form of chloride ___E:ions U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ions)___ , chlorine is necessary to all known species of life. Other types of chlorine compounds are rare in living organisms, and artificially produced chlorinated organics range from inert to toxic.

In the ___E:upper atmosphere U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_atmosphere)___ , chlorine-containing organic molecules such as ___E:chlorofluorocarbons U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chlorofluorocarbon)___ have been implicated in ___E:ozone depletion U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozone_depletion)___ .

Small quantities of elemental chlorine are generated by oxidation of chloride ions in ___E:neutrophils U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutrophil)___ as part of an ___E:immune system U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immune_system)___ response against bacteria.

The most common compound of chlorine, sodium chloride, has been known since ancient times; archaeologists have found evidence that ___E:rock salt U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_salt)___ was used as early as 3000 BC and ___E:brine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brine)___ as early as 6000 BC.

Around 900, the authors of the Arabic writings attributed to ___E:Jabir ibn Hayyan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jabir_ibn_Hayyan)___ (Latin: Geber) and the Persian physician and alchemist ___E:Abu Bakr al-Razi U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Bakr_al-Razi)___ ( c. 865–925, Latin: Rhazes) were experimenting with ___E:sal ammoniac U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sal_ammoniac)___ ( ___E:ammonium chloride U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ammonium_chloride)___ ), which when it was distilled together with ___E:vitriol U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vitriol)___ (hydrated ___E:sulfates U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sulfates)___ of various metals) produced ___E:hydrogen chloride U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen_chloride)___ .

However, it appears that in these early experiments with chloride ___E:salts U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salt_(chemistry))___ , the gaseous products were discarded, and hydrogen chloride may have been produced many times before it was discovered that it can be put to chemical use.  One of the first such uses was the synthesis of ___E:mercury(II) chloride U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury(II)_chloride)___ (corrosive sublimate), whose production from the heating of ___E:mercury U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(element))___ either with ___E:alum U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alum)___ and ammonium chloride or with vitriol and sodium chloride was first described in the De aluminibus et salibus ("On Alums and Salts", an eleventh- or twelfth century Arabic text falsely attributed to Abu Bakr al-Razi and ___E:translated into Latin in the second half of the twelfth century U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_translations_of_the_12th_century)___ by ___E:Gerard of Cremona U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerard_of_Cremona)___ , 1144–1187).

Another important development was the discovery by ___E:pseudo-Geber U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudo-Geber)___ (in the De inventione veritatis , "On the Discovery of Truth", after c. 1300) that by adding ammonium chloride to ___E:nitric acid U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitric_acid)___ , a strong solvent capable of dissolving gold (i.e., aqua regia ) could be produced.

Although aqua regia is an unstable mixture that continually gives off fumes containing free chlorine gas, this chlorine gas appears to have been ignored until c. 1630, when its nature as a separate gaseous substance was recognised by the ___E:Brabantian U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duchy_of_Brabant)___ chemist and physician ___E:Jan Baptist van Helmont U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Baptist_van_Helmont)___ . The element was first studied in detail in 1774 by Swedish chemist ___E:Carl Wilhelm Scheele U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Wilhelm_Scheele)___ , and he is credited with the discovery.
Scheele produced chlorine by reacting ___E:MnO2 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manganese_dioxide)___ (as the mineral ___E:pyrolusite U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrolusite)___ ) with HCl:

Scheele observed several of the properties of chlorine: the bleaching effect on ___E:litmus U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Litmus_test_(chemistry))___ , the deadly effect on insects, the yellow-green colour, and the smell similar to ___E:aqua regia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aqua_regia)___ .

He called it " dephlogisticated muriatic acid air " since it is a gas (then called "airs") and it came from ___E:hydrochloric acid U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrochloric_acid)___ (then known as "muriatic acid").
He failed to establish chlorine as an element.

Common chemical theory at that time held that an acid is a compound that contains oxygen (remnants of this survive in the German and Dutch names of ___E:oxygen U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygen)___ : sauerstoff or zuurstof , both translating into English as acid substance ), so a number of chemists, including ___E:Claude Berthollet U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Berthollet)___ , suggested that Scheele's dephlogisticated muriatic acid air must be a combination of oxygen and the yet undiscovered element, muriaticum .

In 1809, ___E:Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Louis_Gay-Lussac)___ and ___E:Louis-Jacques Thénard U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis-Jacques_Th%C3%A9nard)___ tried to decompose dephlogisticated muriatic acid air by reacting it with charcoal to release the free element muriaticum (and carbon dioxide).
They did not succeed and published a report in which they considered the possibility that dephlogisticated muriatic acid air is an element, but were not convinced.
In 1810, ___E:Sir Humphry Davy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_Humphry_Davy)___ tried the same experiment again, and concluded that the substance was an element, and not a compound.

He announced his results to the Royal Society on 15 November that year.  At that time, he named this new element "chlorine", from the Greek word χλωρος ( chlōros , "green-yellow"), in reference to its colour.

The name " ___E:halogen U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halogen)___ ", meaning "salt producer", was originally used for chlorine in 1811 by ___E:Johann Salomo Christoph Schweigger U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johann_Salomo_Christoph_Schweigger)___ .

This term was later used as a generic term to describe all the elements in the chlorine family (fluorine, bromine, iodine), after a suggestion by ___E:Jöns Jakob Berzelius U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J%C3%B6ns_Jakob_Berzelius)___ in 1826.   In 1823, ___E:Michael Faraday U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Faraday)___ liquefied chlorine for the first time,    and demonstrated that what was then known as "solid chlorine" had a structure of ___E:chlorine hydrate U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clathrate_hydrate)___ (Cl 2 ·H 2 O).

Chlorine gas was first used by French chemist ___E:Claude Berthollet U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Louis_Berthollet)___ to bleach textiles in 1785.   Modern bleaches resulted from further work by Berthollet, who first produced ___E:sodium hypochlorite U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodium_hypochlorite)___ in 1789 in his laboratory in the town of ___E:Javel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Javel_-_Andr%C3%A9_Citro%C3%ABn_(Paris_M%C3%A9tro))___ (now part of Paris, France), by passing chlorine gas through a solution of sodium carbonate.

The resulting liquid, known as " Eau de Javel " (" ___E:Javel water U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Javel_water)___ "), was a weak solution of ___E:sodium hypochlorite U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodium_hypochlorite)___ .
This process was not very efficient, and alternative production methods were sought.

Scottish chemist and industrialist ___E:Charles Tennant U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Tennant)___ first produced a solution of ___E:calcium hypochlorite U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calcium_hypochlorite)___ ("chlorinated lime"), then solid calcium hypochlorite (bleaching powder).

These compounds produced low levels of elemental chlorine and could be more efficiently transported than sodium hypochlorite, which remained as dilute solutions because when purified to eliminate water, it became a dangerously powerful and unstable oxidiser.
Near the end of the nineteenth century, E. S.

Smith patented a method of sodium hypochlorite production involving electrolysis of ___E:brine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brine)___ to produce ___E:sodium hydroxide U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodium_hydroxide)___ and chlorine gas, which then mixed to form sodium hypochlorite.

This is known as the ___E:chloralkali process U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chloralkali_process)___ , first introduced on an industrial scale in 1892, and now the source of most elemental chlorine and sodium hydroxide.
In 1884 Chemischen Fabrik Griesheim of Germany developed another ___E:chloralkali process U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chloralkali_process)___ which entered commercial production in 1888.

Elemental chlorine solutions dissolved in ___E:chemically basic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Base_(chemistry))___ water (sodium and ___E:calcium hypochlorite U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calcium_hypochlorite)___ ) were first used as anti- ___E:putrefaction U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Putrefaction)___ agents and ___E:disinfectants U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disinfectant)___ in the 1820s, in France, long before the establishment of the ___E:germ theory of disease U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germ_theory_of_disease)___ .

This practice was pioneered by ___E:Antoine-Germain Labarraque U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antoine-Germain_Labarraque)___ , who adapted Berthollet's "Javel water" bleach and other chlorine preparations.

Elemental chlorine has since served a continuous function in topical ___E:antisepsis U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antiseptic)___ (wound irrigation solutions and the like) and public sanitation, particularly in swimming and drinking water.

Chlorine gas was first used as a weapon on April 22, 1915, at the ___E:Second Battle of Ypres U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Battle_of_Ypres)___ by the ___E:German Army U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_Army_(German_Empire))___ .
The effect on the allies was devastating because the existing ___E:gas masks U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WWI_gas_mask)___ were difficult to deploy and had not been broadly distributed.
Chlorine is the second ___E:halogen U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halogen)___ , being a ___E:nonmetal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonmetal_(chemistry))___ in group 17 of the periodic table.

Its properties are thus similar to ___E:fluorine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fluorine)___ , ___E:bromine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bromine)___ , and ___E:iodine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iodine)___ , and are largely intermediate between those of the first two. Chlorine has the electron configuration [Ne]3s 2 3p 5 , with the seven electrons in the third and outermost shell acting as its ___E:valence electrons U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valence_electron)___ .
Like all halogens, it is thus one electron short of a full octet, and is hence a strong oxidising agent, reacting with many elements in order to complete its outer shell.

Corresponding to ___E:periodic trends U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Periodic_trend)___ , it is intermediate in ___E:electronegativity U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronegativity)___ between fluorine and bromine (F: 3.98, Cl: 3.16, Br: 2.96, I: 2.66), and is less reactive than fluorine and more reactive than bromine.
It is also a weaker oxidising agent than fluorine, but a stronger one than bromine.
Conversely, the ___E:chloride U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chloride)___ ion is a weaker reducing agent than bromide, but a stronger one than fluoride.

It is intermediate in ___E:atomic radius U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_radius)___ between fluorine and bromine, and this leads to many of its atomic properties similarly continuing the trend from iodine to bromine upward, such as first ___E:ionisation energy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ionisation_energy)___ , ___E:electron affinity U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electron_affinity)___ , enthalpy of dissociation of the X 2 molecule (X = Cl, Br, I), ionic radius, and X–X bond length. (Fluorine is anomalous due to its small size.)

All four stable halogens experience intermolecular ___E:van der Waals forces U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_der_Waals_force)___ of attraction, and their strength increases together with the number of electrons among all homonuclear diatomic halogen molecules.

Thus, the melting and boiling points of chlorine are intermediate between those of fluorine and bromine: chlorine melts at −101.0 °C and boils at −34.0 °C. As a result of the increasing molecular weight of the halogens down the group, the density and heats of fusion and vaporisation of chlorine are again intermediate between those of bromine and fluorine, although all their heats of vaporisation are fairly low (leading to high volatility) thanks to their diatomic molecular structure.
The halogens darken in colour as the group is descended: thus, while fluorine is a pale yellow gas, chlorine is distinctly yellow-green.
This trend occurs because the wavelengths of visible light absorbed by the halogens increase down the group.

Specifically, the colour of a halogen, such as chlorine, results from the ___E:electron transition U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_electron_transition)___ between the ___E:highest occupied U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HOMO/LUMO)___ antibonding πg molecular orbital and the lowest vacant antibonding σu molecular orbital.
The colour fades at low temperatures, so that solid chlorine at −195 °C is almost colourless.

Like solid bromine and iodine, solid chlorine crystallises in the ___E:orthorhombic crystal system U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orthorhombic_crystal_system)___ , in a layered lattice of Cl 2 molecules.

The Cl–Cl distance is 198 pm (close to the gaseous Cl–Cl distance of 199 pm) and the Cl···Cl distance between molecules is 332 pm within a layer and 382 pm between layers (compare the van der Waals radius of chlorine, 180 pm).
This structure means that chlorine is a very poor conductor of electricity, and indeed its conductivity is so low as to be practically unmeasurable.
Chlorine has two stable isotopes, 35 Cl and 37 Cl. These are its only two natural isotopes occurring in quantity, with 35 Cl making up 76% of natural chlorine and 37 Cl making up the remaining 24%.

Both are synthesised in stars in the ___E:oxygen-burning U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygen-burning_process)___ and ___E:silicon-burning processes U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon-burning_process)___ .

Both have nuclear spin 3/2+ and thus may be used for ___E:nuclear magnetic resonance U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_magnetic_resonance)___ , although the spin magnitude being greater than 1/2 results in non-spherical nuclear charge distribution and thus resonance broadening as a result of a nonzero ___E:nuclear quadrupole moment U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_quadrupole_moment)___ and resultant quadrupolar relaxation.

The other chlorine isotopes are all radioactive, with ___E:half-lives U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half-life)___ too short to occur in nature ___E:primordially U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primordial_element)___ .

Of these, the most commonly used in the laboratory are 36 Cl ( t 1/2 = 3.0×10 5 y) and 38 Cl ( t 1/2 = 37.2 min), which may be produced from the ___E:neutron activation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutron_activation)___ of natural chlorine.

The most stable chlorine radioisotope is 36 Cl. The primary decay mode of isotopes lighter than 35 Cl is ___E:electron capture U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electron_capture)___ to isotopes of ___E:sulfur U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sulfur)___ ; that of isotopes heavier than 37 Cl is ___E:beta decay U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beta_decay)___ to isotopes of ___E:argon U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argon)___ ; and 36 Cl may decay by either mode to stable 36 S or 36 Ar.  ___E:36Cl U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chlorine-36)___ occurs in trace quantities in nature as a ___E:cosmogenic nuclide U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmogenic_nuclide)___ in a ratio of about (7–10) × 10 −13 to 1 with stable chlorine isotopes: it is produced in the atmosphere by ___E:spallation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spallation)___ of 36 ___E:Ar U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argon)___ by interactions with ___E:cosmic ray U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_ray)___ ___E:protons U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proton)___ .

In the top meter of the ___E:lithosphere U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lithosphere)___ , 36 Cl is generated primarily by ___E:thermal neutron U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thermal_neutron)___ activation of 35 Cl and spallation of 39 ___E:K U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potassium)___ and 40 ___E:Ca U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calcium)___ .

In the subsurface environment, ___E:muon capture U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muon_capture)___ by 40 ___E:Ca U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calcium)___ becomes more important as a way to generate 36 Cl.
Chlorine is intermediate in reactivity between fluorine and bromine, and is one of the most reactive elements.
Chlorine is a weaker oxidising agent than fluorine but a stronger one than bromine or iodine.

This can be seen from the ___E:standard electrode potentials U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_electrode_potential)___ of the X 2 /X − couples (F, +2.866 V; Cl, +1.395 V; Br, +1.087 V; I, +0.615 V; ___E:At U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astatine)___ , approximately +0.3 V).

However, this trend is not shown in the bond energies because fluorine is singular due to its small size, low polarisability, and inability to show ___E:hypervalence U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypervalence)___ .

As another difference, chlorine has a significant chemistry in positive oxidation states while fluorine does not. Chlorination often leads to higher oxidation states than bromination or iodination but lower oxidation states than fluorination.
Chlorine tends to react with compounds including M–M, M–H, or M–C bonds to form M–Cl bonds.

The simplest chlorine compound is ___E:hydrogen chloride U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen_chloride)___ , HCl, a major chemical in industry as well as in the laboratory, both as a gas and dissolved in water as ___E:hydrochloric acid U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrochloric_acid)___ .
It is often produced by burning hydrogen gas in chlorine gas, or as a byproduct of chlorinating ___E:hydrocarbons U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrocarbon)___ .

Another approach is to treat ___E:sodium chloride U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodium_chloride)___ with concentrated ___E:sulfuric acid U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sulfuric_acid)___ to produce hydrochloric acid, also known as the "salt-cake" process:

In the laboratory, hydrogen chloride gas may be made by drying the acid with concentrated sulfuric acid. Deuterium chloride, DCl, may be produced by reacting ___E:benzoyl chloride U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benzoyl_chloride)___ with ___E:heavy water U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heavy_water)___ (D 2 O).

At room temperature, hydrogen chloride is a colourless gas, like all the hydrogen halides apart from ___E:hydrogen fluoride U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen_fluoride)___ , since hydrogen cannot form strong ___E:hydrogen bonds U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen_bond)___ to the larger electronegative chlorine atom; however, weak hydrogen bonding is present in solid crystalline hydrogen chloride at low temperatures, similar to the hydrogen fluoride structure, before disorder begins to prevail as the temperature is raised.
Hydrochloric acid is a strong acid (p K a = −7) because the hydrogen-chlorine bonds are too weak to inhibit dissociation.
The HCl/H 2 O system has many hydrates HCl· n H 2 O for n = 1, 2, 3, 4, and 6. Beyond a 1:1 mixture of HCl and H 2 O, the system separates completely into two separate liquid phases.

Hydrochloric acid forms an ___E:azeotrope U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azeotrope)___ with boiling point 108.58 °C at 20.22 g HCl per 100 g solution; thus hydrochloric acid cannot be concentrated beyond this point by distillation.

Unlike hydrogen fluoride, anhydrous liquid hydrogen chloride is difficult to work with as a solvent, because its boiling point is low, it has a small liquid range, its ___E:dielectric constant U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dielectric_constant)___ is low and it does not dissociate appreciably into H 2 Cl + and HCl−2 ions – the latter, in any case, are much less stable than the ___E:bifluoride U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bifluoride)___ ions ( HF−2 ) due to the very weak hydrogen bonding between hydrogen and chlorine, though its salts with very large and weakly polarising cations such as ___E:Cs+ U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caesium)___ and ___E:NR+4 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quaternary_ammonium_cation)___ (R = ___E:Me U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methyl_group)___ , ___E:Et U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethyl_group)___ , ___E:Bun U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Butyl_group)___ ) may still be isolated.

However, the extent of chlorination is difficult to control: the reaction is not ___E:regioselective U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regioselectivity)___ and often results in a mixture of various isomers with different degrees of chlorination, though this may be permissible if the products are easily separated.

The ___E:haloform reaction U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haloform_reaction)___ , using chlorine and ___E:sodium hydroxide U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodium_hydroxide)___ , is also able to generate alkyl halides from methyl ketones, and related compounds.

Many organochlorine compounds have been isolated from natural sources ranging from bacteria to humans.

Chlorinated organic compounds are found in nearly every class of biomolecules including ___E:alkaloids U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alkaloid)___ , ___E:terpenes U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terpene)___ , ___E:amino acids U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amino_acid)___ , ___E:flavonoids U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flavonoid)___ , ___E:steroids U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steroid)___ , and ___E:fatty acids U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fatty_acid)___ .

Organochlorides, including ___E:dioxins U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polychlorinated_dibenzodioxins)___ , are produced in the high temperature environment of forest fires, and dioxins have been found in the preserved ashes of lightning-ignited fires that predate synthetic dioxins.

In addition, a variety of simple chlorinated hydrocarbons including dichloromethane, chloroform, and ___E:carbon tetrachloride U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_tetrachloride)___ have been isolated from marine algae.

Some types of organochlorides, though not all, have significant toxicity to plants or animals, including humans.

Dioxins, produced when organic matter is burned in the presence of chlorine, and some ___E:insecticides U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insecticide)___ , such as ___E:DDT U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DDT)___ , are ___E:persistent organic pollutants U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persistent_organic_pollutant)___ which pose dangers when they are released into the environment.

For example, DDT, which was widely used to control insects in the mid 20th century, also accumulates in food chains, and causes reproductive problems (e.g., eggshell thinning) in certain bird species.

Chlorine is too reactive to occur as the free element in nature but is very abundant in the form of its chloride salts.

It is the 20th most abundant element  in Earth's crust and makes up 126 ___E:parts per million U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parts_per_million)___ of it, through the large deposits of chloride minerals, especially ___E:sodium chloride U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodium_chloride)___ , that have been evaporated from water bodies.
